proof.text: For an object $W\to V$ put $W_X=W\times_V X$ and $W_Z=W\times_V Z$. The open-immersion base-change lemma identifies these with the inverse images in $W$ of the two complementary opens of $V$. Hence they are complementary open subschemes and $W=W_X\amalg W_Z$. Applying weakly-etale base change to $W\to V$ shows that $W_X\to X$ and $W_Z\to Z$ are objects of the respective small pro-etale sites. Open immersions are objects of the pro-etale site, as specified in the localization lemma. The family $\{W_X,W_Z\}\to W$ is a Zariski covering, hence a pro-etale covering by the explicit covering clause of [sk-def-pe-site]. The localization lemma identifies restriction along $s,t$ with evaluation on these component sites and identifies their coefficient sheaves with the restrictions of $A_V$.

proof.text: For every module sheaf $F$ on $V$ its restriction map $F(W)\to F(W_X)\times F(W_Z)$ is bijective: the sheaf equalizer for the cover of step 1 has no cross-component compatibility conditions, because $W_X\times_W W_Z=\varnothing$ and $F(\varnothing)=0$ by the empty-cover sheaf condition; the same-component conditions are identities. This bijection is additive and $A_V(W)$-linear through the two coefficient restriction maps. It is natural in $W$ and $F$, since both maps are restrictions of sections.

source.place: First sentence: disjoint open cover and sheaf gluing axiom; explicit equalizer argument

proof.text: For module sheaves $M$ on $X$ and $N$ on $Z$ define $G(M,N)(W)=M(W_X)\times N(W_Z)$, with componentwise restrictions and $A_V(W)$-action through restriction of coefficients. For a covering $\{W_i\to W\}$, its pullbacks to $W_X,W_Z$ are coverings of the component sites. A matching family for $G$ is exactly a pair of matching families for $M,N$, and each has one unique amalgamation. Thus $G$ is a module sheaf. On an object lying entirely over $X$ the second factor is $N(\varnothing)=0$, so $s^*G(M,N)=M$, and similarly $t^*G(M,N)=N$. The maps in step 2 give $F\cong G(s^*F,t^*F)$. Products of maps give the inverse on morphisms; restriction of these two natural isomorphisms is the identity on both components. This constructs the asserted additive equivalence, not just a bijection on isomorphism classes.

source.place: First sentence: explicit quasi-inverse for the disjoint-open-cover description

proof.text: The functor $\Phi:F\mapsto(s^*F,t^*F)$ of step 3 is an additive equivalence with explicit quasi-inverse $G$. The product of the two abelian module-sheaf categories is abelian, with kernels and cokernels computed coordinatewise: a map into or out of the pair of kernels (resp. cokernels) has the required universal factorization exactly in each coordinate. An equivalence of categories carries a kernel (resp. cokernel) diagram to a kernel (resp. cokernel) diagram, since the universal property is a statement about Hom sets, which $\Phi$ and $G$ biject. Hence $\Phi$ and $G$ preserve kernels and cokernels, i.e. are exact, and so are $s^*=\mathrm{pr}_1\Phi$ and $t^*=\mathrm{pr}_2\Phi$, because the coordinate projections preserve the coordinatewise kernels and cokernels. No comparison of restriction with the inverse image of a morphism of sites is used.

source.place: First sentence: exactness of the product description

proof.text: In the product category, maps $(M,0)\to(F_X,F_Z)$ are exactly maps $M\to F_X$, since there is a unique map $0\to F_Z$. Consequently $G(M,0)$ is left adjoint to restriction to $X$. The stated extension-by-zero adjunction says that the specific $s_!$ of the item is another left adjoint to the same restriction. The unique adjunction-compatible isomorphism therefore identifies $s_!M$ with $G(M,0)$: explicitly it is the map corresponding to $1_M$ under the two Hom bijections, and its inverse is obtained the same way; the composites correspond to $1_M$ and hence are identities. In particular its restriction to $X$ is the canonical identification with $M$. This specifies the identification, including the restriction map used below.

source.place: Second sentence: extension by zero is insertion into the first component

proof.text: Apply the additive equivalence and $G$ in every degree to complexes and their differentials. The identities $d^{n+1}d^n=0$ and $d_F^n a^n=a^{n+1}d_E^n$ hold exactly when they hold in each component, so this gives inverse equivalences on all integer-indexed cochain complexes. By exactness from step 4 and the kernel/image definition of cohomology, $H^n(E)$ goes to $(H^n(s^*E),H^n(t^*E))$. Acyclicity is therefore componentwise. Finally, the homotopy equation $a^n-b^n=d^{n-1}h^n+h^{n+1}d^n$ is componentwise because the equivalence preserves addition and composition. No degree bound or infinite totalization is involved.

source.place: Section 010V (homology-section-complexes), cochain and cohomology definitions; derived.tex Definition 070H (definition-K-injective) for homotopies

proof.text: Let $E$ be an acyclic complex on $V$ and $a:E\to s_!I$ a chain map. By steps 5 and 6 it is the pair $(a_X:s^*E\to I,0:t^*E\to0)$, with $s^*E$ acyclic. Since $I$ is K-injective there is $h_X$ satisfying $a_X=dh_X+h_Xd$. The pair $(h_X,0)$ satisfies $a=d(h_X,0)+(h_X,0)d$ componentwise. Applying $G$ and the natural component identifications gives a null homotopy of the original map. This is precisely the definition of K-injectivity of $s_!I$, for arbitrary unbounded $E$ and $I$.

source.place: Definition 070H (definition-K-injective); the null-homotopy argument of Lemma 08BJ (lemma-adjoint-preserve-K-injectives), written explicitly for the product

proof.text: For an object $W\to X$, the direct-image definition gives $(q_*s_!M)(W)=(s_!M)(V\times_X W)$. The two components of $V\times_X W$ are $s(X)\times_X W\cong W$ (because $q\circ s=1_X$) and $Z\times_X W$. Steps 2 and 5 identify its sections with $M(W)\times0$, and restriction to the first component is the first projection, an isomorphism to $M(W)$. The isomorphism $s(X)\times_X W\cong W$ is over $X$, so the composite coefficient map $A_X(W)\to A_V(V\times_X W)\to A_X(W)$ is the identity: on constant presheaf sections both arrows send $a$ to $a$, and their composite after the sheafification unit is the identity constant-section map. The universal property defining the extension to the constant ring sheaf makes the composite the identity. Thus the projection is $A_X(W)$-linear. For $W^\prime\to W$ both routes in the naturality square are restriction to $W^\prime$; for $M\to M^\prime$ both are its component map on $W$. This gives the stated natural sheaf isomorphism. In each degree it commutes with the differential and every component of a chain map or degree-minus-one homotopy by this naturality. Hence the same formula gives the asserted isomorphism of complexes and its compatibility with homotopies.

title: Clopen pro-etale component decomposition and K-injective insertion
statement:
Let $X,V$ be schemes [def-pc-scheme], let $q:V\to X$ be a scheme morphism, and let $s:X\hookrightarrow V$ be an open immersion [def-weil-open-immersion] with closed image and $qs=1_X$. Put $Z=V\setminus s(X)$ with open inclusion $t:Z\hookrightarrow V$. For a finite commutative ring $A$, use module sheaves over the constant coefficient sheaves on the small pro-etale sites [def-weil-pbc-proetale-site, def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category]. Restriction gives an exact equivalence
$$\operatorname{Mod}(V_{\mathrm{proet}},A)\simeq\operatorname{Mod}(X_{\mathrm{proet}},A)\times\operatorname{Mod}(Z_{\mathrm{proet}},A),\qquad F\mapsto(s^*F,t^*F),$$
under which extension by zero $s_!$ [def-weil-extension-by-zero] is the insertion $M\mapsto(M,0)$. The induced equivalence on unbounded cochain complexes carries acyclic complexes and chain homotopies componentwise. In particular, if $I$ is K-injective on $X_{\mathrm{proet}}$ [def-pur-kinjective-complex], then $s_!I$ is K-injective on $V_{\mathrm{proet}}$. The ordinary direct image of [def-weil-proetale-module-direct-image] has a natural isomorphism $q_*s_!M\cong M$ for every module sheaf $M$: on each site object $W\to X$ its map is restriction of sections on $V\times_XW$ to the component $s(X)\times_XW\cong W$. This isomorphism extends termwise to complexes and commutes with chain maps and homotopies.
